newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway's central bank cuts key interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Norway's central bank cuts key interest rates.

text.p: Norway's central bank announced on Tuesday it was cutting its key interest rates, effective on Wednesday, to rein in the strong crown.

The bank said it was trimming its overnight deposit rate, the credit rate, to 4.0 percent from 4.50 percent. The overnight lending rate, charged to commercial and savings banks, was reduced to 6.0 percent from 6.50 percent.

The crown has strengthened rapidly because of soaring oil prices the wide gap in interest rate differentials between Norway and other European markets. Norway is the world's second-biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia.
At the close of trade on Tuesday, interest rate differential between Norwegian and German three-month swap rates had narrowed sharply to 150 basis points from 190.
Meanwhile the crown weakened to 101.54 on the reverse ECU index, a weighted currency basket, by the close of business compared with 101.17 at 1130 GMT just before the announcement.
Dealers said the the market had been increasingly nervous over the crown's relentless rise.
"We smelled blood this morning as the crown continued to appreciate so strongly," said one dealer. "Something had to happen."
Central Bank Governor Kjell Storvik said in a statement the decision came in response to recent developments in the money and foreign exchange markets.
"The crown exchange rate has been under persistent pressure and the Norwegian Bank has purchased considerable amounts of foreign currency to curb the rise in the crown exchange rate," Storvik said.
"A reduction in Norges Bank's interest rates now seemed appropriate to reduce the appreciation pressure."

The bank has sold more than 60 billion Norwegian crowns ($9.46 billion) on the foreign exchange markets so far this year, partly to curb the crown's strengthening and partly to cover investments for the state petroleum fund into which the country's 1996 budget surplus will be invested.
The primary objective of Norwegian monetary policy is exchange rate stability, but the bank has been worried about cutting rates due to fears of rising inflation.

"I am not very surprised, but I had thought they would hold out a bit longer," said Marius Loemo, a macro economist in Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse. "But it is clear that the crowns's strength had started approaching levels where it is difficult to say it is compatible with a stable currency."
"This underscores the necessity to push through a tight budget," he said.

Storvik repeated his stance that fiscal policy must assume the main responsibility for stabilising the economy. The central bank head has urged parliament not to dilute the 1997 state budget and risk higher cost growth next year.

The budget is projected to show a surplus of 40.9 billion crowns in 1997, but the government has said it will keep a tight grip on expenditure for fear of fuelling inflation. A majority in parliament, however, wants to raise spending.
The rate on overnight deposits at the central bank sets the floor for money market rates and the overnight lending rate sets the ceiling for them.
On March 7 the central bank last trimmed both key rates by 0.25 percentage points, the first key interest rate cut since February 1994. ($1=6.343 Norwegian Crown)
